\chapter{Noise, Silence, Calm and Hurry}
\label{ch:calma-y-prisa}
\hlchaptermodality{333}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say el ruido, el silencio, la calma, la prisa and el cuidado, and say why a word for burning heat came to mean stillness.}

Complete ES-C333-cuidado: answer ruido with silencio, ask for calma, take the prisa out of a moment, and say cuidado when it matters.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el ruido]{el ruido — noise, from the roaring of lions}

\label{lesson:ES-C333-ruido}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the word}, then \emph{the voice}. (\emph{La palabra}; \emph{la voz}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la voz — the sound this one drowns out.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{RUI-do}, two beats with the weight on the first. The initial \emph{r} is rolled, and \emph{ui} is a single glide, not two separate vowels. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el ruido} — \textquotedblleft{}the noise.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{rugīre} meant \emph{to roar}, and Roman writers used it of lions. The noun \textbf{rugītus} was \emph{a roaring}. Spanish wore the \emph{g} away entirely and arrived at \textbf{ruido}, and along the way the meaning shrank from a lion's roar to any unwanted sound at all — traffic, a bad connection, a room too full of people.

That is a long fall in volume for one word, and it is worth hearing the original inside it. When Spanish says \emph{hay mucho ruido}, the word underneath is still a lion.

Spanish also kept a closer descendant, \textbf{rugido}, which is still \emph{a roar} and is what a lion does in a Spanish book. So the language has the word twice: once worn down and generalised, once preserved and specific. You met that pattern with \emph{cosa} and \emph{causa}.

English did receive the root, in an unlikely place. \textbf{Rut} — the season when stags bellow and fight — came through Old French \emph{rut} from this same \emph{rugītus}. The English word kept the roaring and lost the noise; the Spanish word kept the noise and lost the roaring.

\emph{Ruido} is also the word for \textbf{noise} in the technical sense, the unwanted signal in a measurement, which is one of those places where Spanish and English happen to have reached for the same metaphor.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five words for how loud or how rushed a moment is.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el ruido}
  \item \emph{mucho ruido}
  \item \emph{sin ruido}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{rugīre} mean, and of which animal? (To roar — of lions.) And which English word for a deer's season comes from it? (\emph{Rut}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el silencio]{el silencio — the one word here English took without changing it}

\label{lesson:ES-C333-silencio}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the voice}, then \emph{the noise}. (\emph{La voz}; \emph{el ruido}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el ruido — the word this one answers.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{si-LEN-cio}, four beats with the weight on \emph{-LEN-}. The \emph{c} before \emph{i} is soft — an \emph{s} across the Americas, a \emph{th} in much of Spain — and \emph{-cio} runs together as one glide. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el silencio} — \textquotedblleft{}the silence.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{silēre} meant \emph{to be still, to say nothing}, and \textbf{silentium} was the state of doing so. Spanish and English are looking at almost the same letters here, which makes this the easiest word in the chapter and a good place to say why that happens.

Most English words from Latin arrived through French, battered by centuries of French mouths, and come out looking different from their Spanish cousins. \emph{Palabra} and \emph{parable} barely resemble each other. But \textbf{silence} and \textbf{silentium} and \textbf{silencio} line up because the word was rare enough, and formal enough, that it was largely carried in writing rather than in speech. Written words do not wear down.

The pair in English splits neatly. \textbf{Silence}, the noun, came through French. \textbf{Silent}, the adjective, is the Latin present participle \emph{silēns, silentis} taken straight. And the same Latin participle gives Spanish nothing extra — it uses \textbf{callado} or \textbf{en silencio} where English says \emph{silent}.

Note that \emph{silencio} is a \textbf{thing}, not a state you are in. Spanish says \textbf{estar en silencio}, to be \emph{in} silence, the way you would be in a room.

And \emph{silencio} on its own, said sharply, is what a teacher says to a class.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two of five. Noise and its absence, and you can now name either.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el silencio}
  \item \emph{en silencio}
  \item \emph{silencio, por favor}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{silēre} mean? (To be still, to say nothing.) And why do \emph{silence} and \emph{silencio} look so alike? (The word travelled in writing, not worn down by speech.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la calma]{la calma — calm began as the burning heat of noon}

\label{lesson:ES-C333-calma}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the noise}, then \emph{the silence}. (\emph{El ruido}; \emph{el silencio}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el silencio — the quiet this one describes from the inside.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{CAL-ma}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{c} before \emph{a} is a hard \emph{k}, and the \emph{l} is light with the tongue tip forward. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la calma} — \textquotedblleft{}the calm,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the stillness.\textquotedblright{}

This word did not start out peaceful. It started out \textbf{hot}.

Greek \textbf{kaûma} meant \emph{burning heat}, from \textbf{kaíein}, \emph{to burn}. Late Latin borrowed it as \textbf{cauma}, still meaning the heat of the day.

The shift happened at sea. In the Mediterranean the hottest hours are the ones when the wind drops and a sailing ship cannot move — the burning noon and the dead air arrive together. Sailors talking about \emph{cauma} were talking about the heat, but what mattered to them was the \textbf{stillness} that came with it. Over time the word stopped naming the temperature and started naming the calm.

You can still hear the old meaning in the English phrase \textbf{dead calm}, and in the word \textbf{doldrums} for a windless band of ocean — a place named entirely by what it stops you doing.

English \textbf{calm} was borrowed from Romance with the shift already complete, so English never had the hot sense at all. Spanish keeps the family: \textbf{calmar} is to calm, and \textbf{calmado} is calmed.

Two phrases to have. \textbf{Con calma} is \emph{calmly, take your time}, and it is one of the kindest things you can say to somebody who is flustered. And \textbf{¡calma!} on its own is \emph{steady on}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three of five. And one of them is a weather report that turned into a mood.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la calma}
  \item \emph{con calma}
  \item \emph{calma, por favor}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Greek \emph{kaûma} mean? (Burning heat.) And why did a word for heat come to mean stillness? (At sea the hottest hours are the windless ones.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la prisa]{la prisa — hurry is being pressed}

\label{lesson:ES-C333-prisa}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the silence}, then \emph{the calm}. (\emph{El silencio}; \emph{la calma}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la calma — the word this one is the opposite of.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{PRI-sa}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{pr} is a tight cluster with no vowel between the letters, and the \emph{r} is a single tap. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la prisa} — \textquotedblleft{}the hurry,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the rush.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{premere} meant \emph{to press}, and \textbf{pressa} was its feminine past participle: \emph{pressed}. Spanish took that participle and made a noun of it.

So Spanish does not think of hurry as speed. It thinks of it as \textbf{being under pressure}. The idiom follows the metaphor exactly: you do not \emph{have} hurry, you say \textbf{tengo prisa} — \emph{I have pressure on me} — and \textbf{de prisa} is \emph{under pressure}, meaning quickly.

English has the same root in a dozen shapes, and the squeeze is audible in all of them. To \textbf{press} is the plain verb. \textbf{Pressure} is the noun. To \textbf{express} is to press out — which is what you do to a thought, and also what an espresso machine does to coffee. To \textbf{impress} is to press into, leaving a mark. To \textbf{oppress} is to press against. To \textbf{compress} is to press together. To \textbf{suppress} is to press down. A \textbf{printing} press pressed letters into paper, which is why \textbf{print} is the same word worn short.

And \textbf{espresso} is Italian for \emph{pressed out}, named for the method, not the speed — though almost everybody now hears the \emph{express} in it and assumes it means fast.

The most useful phrase is \textbf{sin prisa} — \emph{unhurried}, and a good thing to say to somebody who is apologising for being slow.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four of five. Loud, quiet, still, and pressed.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la prisa}
  \item \emph{sin prisa}
  \item \emph{tengo prisa}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{premere} mean? (To press.) And what does \emph{tengo prisa} say literally? (I have pressure on me.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el cuidado]{el cuidado — care is a thing you have thought about}

\label{lesson:ES-C333-cuidado}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the calm}, then \emph{the hurry}. (\emph{La calma}; \emph{la prisa}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la prisa — the thing this word warns you against.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{cui-DA-do}, three beats with the weight in the middle. The \emph{cui-} is a hard \emph{k} followed by a \emph{w} glide, and both \emph{d} sounds are soft between vowels. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el cuidado} — \textquotedblleft{}care,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}caution.\textquotedblright{}

The path here is longer than it looks, and better.

Latin \textbf{cōgitāre} meant \emph{to think}. Its past participle \textbf{cōgitātum} was \emph{a thing that has been thought about}. Spanish wore it down — \emph{cogitado}, \emph{cuidado} — and kept the noun.

So \emph{cuidado} is not fear and it is not worry. It is \textbf{thought given to a thing}. To do something \emph{con cuidado} is to do it having thought about it. To \emph{tener cuidado} is to keep a matter in mind. And the verb \textbf{cuidar}, \emph{to look after}, is at root \emph{to keep thinking about} — which is a rather good description of what looking after somebody actually involves.

English has the same verb in \textbf{cogitate}, though it now sounds heavier than plain \emph{think}. And it has the most famous sentence in philosophy: Descartes' \textbf{cogito, ergo sum} — \emph{I think, therefore I am}. That \emph{cogito} is this word. Spanish care and Cartesian doubt are the same Latin verb, one worn smooth by speech and one preserved in a book.

Said sharply and alone, \textbf{¡cuidado!} is the Spanish shout for \emph{watch out} — and even that is, underneath, an instruction to \textbf{think}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five words for the temperature of a moment: \emph{el ruido}, \emph{el silencio}, \emph{la calma}, \emph{la prisa}, \emph{el cuidado}. A noise, its absence, a stillness, a pressure, and a thought.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el cuidado}
  \item \emph{con cuidado}
  \item \emph{cuidado, por favor}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{cōgitāre} mean? (To think.) And which famous sentence is built on it? (\emph{Cogito, ergo sum} — I think, therefore I am.)
\end{tcolorbox}
